text:
This DIN explains MOD rules and approval requirements for contact with parliamentarians, including ministers from other government departments (OGDs). It covers requests for information, contact with parliamentary committees and groups, visits by parliamentarians to defence establishments, and related activities. This DIN applies to MOD service personnel and civilian employees. Contractors, agency staff, and staff of MOD arm’s length bodies (ALBs) and non-departmental public bodies (NDPBs) are expected to comply with its requirements. It applies across the whole force, including Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel and Defence Equipment and Support (DE&S).For brevity, the term “MOD personnel” includes all those listed above.

The term “parliamentarian” is used to apply to all Members of Parliament (MPs), Members of the Devolved Legislatures (MDLs) and active Members of the House of Lords (Peers) (whose names are registered on the UK Parliament website), and their staff. “Ministers” refers to those holding positions within the MOD, including the Secretary of State and other Ministers.

This DIN neither precludes nor imposes any pre-authorisation requirement on:

Contact between MOD personnel acting in their role as an elected representative of a Trade Union (TU) (or other such organisations such as the Defence Police Federation) and relevant parliamentarians on issues relating to their role.

MOD personnel consulting with their constituency parliamentarian in a personal capacity.

MOD personnel raising a concern/whistleblowing via parliamentary channels in accordance with the Raising a Concern policy in JSP 492 (internal access only).

For further guidance as to the scenarios mentioned above, see ‘When you do not need Ministerial approval’ below.

Why this guidance exists

Ministers are accountable to Parliament for the policies, decisions and actions of their departments. Parliamentarians have direct access to ministers. Information requested from the department should be provided by ministers, for example through answers to parliamentary questions. This guidance helps ensure that information provided to Parliament by, or on behalf of, the MOD is accurate and releasable, and that ministers can be assured of that.

MOD personnel are accountable to ministers, not directly to Parliament. Subject to the exceptions under ‘When you do not need Ministerial approval’, MOD personnel must not provide information to parliamentarians or their staff about defence or government matters without ministerial authorisation. For the purposes of this DIN, “defence or government matters” includes official defence or government business, information connected to an individual’s work or workplace, classified information, and responsibilities arising directly from employment or service.

Report any unplanned meeting with a parliamentarian, their staff, or anyone acting on their behalf where defence or government matters are discussed to the relevant minister’s office. Direct any contact from a parliamentarian, whether in person, by telephone, email or letter, to the relevant minister’s office (see ‘Parliamentary questions and ministerial correspondence’).

When you do not need Ministerial approval

Speaking as a member of a TU or Professional Body.

The requirement to obtain prior authorisation before divulging any information about Defence or Government Matters does not apply to personnel who are engaging with parliamentarians in their capacity as accredited representatives of recognised TUs or formal office-holders in recognised Professional Bodies, e.g. the British Medical Association. However, those acting in such a capacity must make clear during any contact with parliamentarians that they are speaking on behalf of these bodies’ business and not on behalf of the MOD.

In all such cases, personnel remain bound by legal and security obligations (including the Official Secrets Act 1989, OPSEC/PERSEC and data protection duties) and must not imply an official MOD position or act in a way that undermine their ability to execute their MOD position in a politically impartial manner. If there is a potential conflict of interest between an elected role and MOD service or employment, personnel should contact Parliamentary Branch for advice. Details on Trade Union and political activities are covered in detail within the MOD’s Conflicts of Interest: Declarations of Outside Interests (internal access only) guidance.

Contact with constituency parliamentarian(s)

When contacting their constituency MP or MDL in a personal capacity, MOD personnel are not acting on behalf of the MOD and do not need prior authorisation under this DIN. This includes where contact relates to matters arising from, or connected with, their service or employment (for example, housing, healthcare or terms and conditions of service – this list is illustrative only). However, personnel should ensure that no sensitive details (e.g. anything above OFFICIAL or anything that may compromise personal or operational security) or any information that may compromise operational effectiveness, national security, international relations or legal obligations are provided during this contact.

If this contact results in a case being raised by the individual’s parliamentarian with the MOD or other Government Departments, the constituent can request that they remain anonymous and this is expected to be respected by their parliamentarian. Details provided to the MOD or other Government Departments will be used solely for the purpose provided and will not be shared with third parties without written consent from the individual concerned.

MPs and MDLs can make confidential enquiries with officials or a government minister on behalf of MOD personnel. MPs and MDLs represent all the people in their local area, whether they voted for them or not; the local MP and/or MDL should always be contacted first to raise an issue at Parliament.

Personnel should consider whether contacting their constituency parliamentarian is the most appropriate way to resolve a workplace concern. Where possible, concerns should first be raised through the chain of command, line management or other internal processes. Personnel may also wish to contact an HR or welfare representative for advice

Raising a concern or whistleblowing

Personnel who raise a concern or make a whistleblowing disclosure through parliamentary channels other than their constituency parliamentarian are not acting on behalf of the MOD and do not need prior authorisation under this DIN. However, personnel must consult the Raising a Concern policy in JSP 492 (internal access only). This guidance explains:

how to raise a concern

when legal protection may apply under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (PIDA)

what constitutes a protected disclosure under PIDA or MOD policy

Although prior authorisation is not required, disciplinary action may still be taken where a disclosure is not considered to be a protected disclosure.

Parliamentarians visiting defence establishments

Approval must be obtained through defence ministers before any visit takes place. Submit visit approval requests through the chain of command to the relevant MOD Secretariat, which will formally submit the request through the Ministers’ Office.

Non-MOD organisations operating from the Defence Estate may invite parliamentarians to visit sites without requiring an approval to be submitted. Such visits must however be notified to the Service or Defence organisation in command of the site in advance of invitations being sent, which in turn must notify the relevant MOD Secretariat as soon as possible.

Constituency representatives

The exception to the above (Parliamentarians visiting defence establishments) is that parliamentarians may visit Defence establishments within their constituency (or a bordering one) without prior approval, although the relevant MOD Secretariat/Service point of contact must still be informed. Visits should have no media involvement.

Where a visit may highlight sensitive issues, the relevant MOD Secretariat should determine whether ministerial approval is required. MOD Secretariats should ensure that they seek Ministerial approval with at least two weeks’ notice wherever possible.

You must obtain ministerial approval before involving the media. Clearly identify all media involvement in the approval request submitted to the minister.

Visits to Cadet Force establishments which are not located on a Defence establishment have separate regulations in JSP 814, Chapter 7 (internal access only).

Permission is not required for any visits related to Armed Forces’ Day or Remembrance Sunday events, or other civic events such as (but not limited to) Freedom of City, Twinning or Festival days.

Where a parliamentarian requires regular access to an establishment, for example as a Regimental Honorary Colonel, arrange a longer-term agreement through the Ministers’ Office via the relevant MOD Secretariat.

Parliamentarians’ office staff are not permitted to visit Defence establishments as they are not elected representatives. This does not apply to clerks of committees who hold a specified apolitical role within Parliament and are expected to accompany visits in support of their committee (but not entitled to undertake visits in their own right) but does apply to APPG staff as they have no formal role.

Security

Parliamentarians visiting Defence establishments must always be escorted. As visitors to a site, parliamentarians must always comply with site/unit security rules, including rules relating to personal electronic devices and the taking/sharing of photographs/videos/recordings.

Travel expenses

Parliamentarians are not entitled to travel and accommodation at the MOD’s expense. They should arrange and pay for their own travel to and from establishments and be charged non-entitled rates for use of Service accommodation. This also applies to members of the HCDC and any other parliamentary committee members. As an exception, Opposition party leaders and Defence spokespersons may travel on Service transport and stay in Service accommodation free of charge when visiting UK Armed Forces deployed on operations.

Invitations to events

Seek advice from the relevant MOD Secretariat before inviting a parliamentarian to an MOD or service event. Attendance may not be appropriate for political or other reasons. The Secretariat will advise accordingly. You may also need advice from Parliamentary Branch or the Minister’s Office for high-profile or politically sensitive events. Do not issue invitations until ministerial approval has been granted.

Secretariats may wish to consider whether a Ministerial submission may be appropriate for some high profile or politically sensitive events where the Minister may require more detailed advice and information than can be provided within the approval request. You should confirm this with the relevant Ministerial Office before providing the submission.

Requests from OGD Ministers

Any approaches made by OGD Ministers’ Private Office to visit a Defence establishment or hold a meeting with those serving in the Armed Forces or under employment with the MOD or Armed Forces must be referred to the relevant MOD Secretariat who will provide guidance on how to seek approval for the contact. No visits or meetings should be arranged until Ministerial approval has been given.

Requests for information

Do not provide information about defence or government matters to parliamentarians or their staff unless it is already publicly available.

Letters or emails from parliamentarians

All correspondence from parliamentarians must receive a ministerial reply. MOD personnel, regardless of seniority, must not reply directly to parliamentarians on behalf of the department. Send all correspondence to the Central Correspondence Unit. The unit will log and allocate it for response. Instructions are available on the Ministers and Parliament internal website.

Parliamentary questions and ministerial correspondence

If branches have any queries about PQs or Ministerial Correspondence received, they should contact the Parliamentary Branch in the first instance for advice. Branches must not contact parliamentarians’ offices directly.

Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology

The Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology (POST) is an office of both Houses of Parliament which provides parliamentarians with impartial assessments of research evidence and analyses of policy issues. Any contact between POST on behalf of the MOD must be through the HCDC Liaison Officer and their team as the sole point of contact. Any information given to POST must be treated in the same way as any other information provided to Parliament and must be cleared by Ministers first.

House of Commons and House of Lords Libraries

Do not provide information that is not already public. Do not undertake new work to respond to these requests. Refer any such requests to Parliamentary Branch.

Parliamentary committees and groups select committees

Any contact made by or on behalf of the MOD with the HCDC, its individual members or with other Select Committees in the House of Commons or House of Lords, or their staffs, must be through the HCDC Liaison Officer in the Parliamentary Branch. Detailed advice will be provided by the HCDC Liaison Officer in advance of attendance to give evidence. However, it is important to remember that when MOD personnel appear before Select Committees as witnesses or provide written evidence to Select Committee inquiries, they do so on behalf of Ministers and with the authorisation of Ministers. This also applies to any and all other Parliamentary Select Committees as well as the HCDC.

In the event that MOD personnel are called upon to give evidence to a Select Committee in another capacity (e.g. as a Trade Union representative, an individual in a non-Reservist occupation, or in a non-MOD voluntary role), they are expected to inform their line management/chain of command for awareness that they will be appearing in their non-MOD role to avoid any confusion. They are requested to ensure that engagement with the Committee and its staff explicitly confirms this; this includes minimising references to their role in Defence to those necessary (if at all) where related to the topic of the session.

On occasion, a committee may request dispensation for MOD personnel to provide written evidence to a specific inquiry in a personal capacity. In such cases, the request will be considered by Ministers, and communication will be made internally to confirm the decision. Personnel must not assume dispensation has been granted until the department confirms this formally. Any dispensation applies only to the specific inquiry concerned, and the terms will be set out when approval is confirmed.

Armed Forces Parliamentary Scheme

Parliamentarians participate in the Armed Forces Parliamentary Scheme (AFPS) to gain first-hand experience of the Armed Forces. They may be embedded in a unit.

In advance of each year’s AFPS course, the single-Service Secretariat responsible for the AFPS will provide a Ministerial submission with a list of MPs and Peers on the scheme and a draft programme of visits for Ministerial approval. Those arranging visits for the AFPS may liaise with those on the scheme in an administrative capacity. To ensure that opportunities are not missed, last minute changes to the programme can be submitted retrospectively.

No information should be provided to AFPS members unless it is already in the public domain; if the parliamentarian requests additional information, they should be directed to the relevant Minister’s Office. If MOD personnel are invited to speak to the AFPS members formally, they should contact their chain of command. Ministerial offices should be informed.

All-Party Parliamentary Groups

An All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) is an informal group of MPs with a particular interest. Such groups do not hold a scrutiny role within Parliament (unlike Select Committees) and have no formal powers. As such, MOD Ministers and officials are not obliged to attend or engage with APPG activities. Careful consideration should be given before committing departmental resources. APPG membership can change frequently, and some members might not be MPs or Peers.

There are APPGs on various countries and topics, and those with a defence interest include Armed Forces, Armed Forces Covenant, Defence and Security issues, Drones, Shipbuilding and Repair, and Veterans. They are usually sponsored by industry or other interest groups, which frequently provide a secretariat function to the APPG comprising employees of the sponsoring company. APPG members and their sponsors are listed on the APPG Register on the Parliament website.

Obtain ministerial approval before attending or speaking at any APPG event, including events open to the public. Invitations should not be made through the single Service engagement officers or directly to officials. A formal written invitation (email or letter) must be sent by the APPG to the relevant Minister, via the HCDC Liaison team. Any direct approaches to named officials should be redirected in accordance with this procedure*. The HCDC Liaison team will then send the invitation to the relevant lead branch to request advice and will arrange a response to the APPG.

*The only exceptions to this process are invitations from the Armed Forces APPG which can be dealt with via the visits approvals process (Section 15) for Ministerial approval.

Any invitation to speak at an APPG event or to brief an APPG must be treated in the same way as an invitation to speak at a public event. Once Ministerial approval has been given, speeches or briefings must be submitted for formal authorisation under the terms of the 2026 Contact with the Media DIN.

Miscellaneous

Other government departments

Obtain approval from the relevant MOD minister before briefing another government minister, whether verbally or in writing. Obtain approval from the Secretary of State’s Office before briefing Cabinet ministers.

OGDs may contact MOD teams directly asking for inputs into Parliamentary Questions or Ministerial Correspondence. All such requests should be directed through the Parliamentary Branch.

Routine cross-government functions, such as the Home Office Royal and Ministerial Visits Team that support Ministerial overseas visits, do not need approval where the relevant private office is already involved. If contacted unexpectedly by one of these teams, Parliamentary Branch can provide advice and identify the appropriate point of contact.

Political Activity

Any visits made by parliamentarians must take place on the understanding that they cannot be used for political purposes. Commanding Officers and heads of establishment must be impartial in their dealings with all parties.

Parliamentary or Assembly Candidates during an Election Period

When a Parliament or Assembly is dissolved, its members cease to be MPs or MDLs (Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland representatives) and are treated as any other member of the public, with the exception of Ministers who retain their role during this time. Candidates seeking election, from all parties, are treated as members of the public and are not to be afforded any treatment over and above that generally available to members of the public until they become elected. The Permanent Secretary’s office will promulgate Cabinet Office Election Guidance to the Department.

Members of the House of Lords remain so following the dissolution Parliament and so visits involving active Peers should continue to follow the guidance above. Committees of the House of Lords do not function during the dissolution period so any planned visits should be postponed.

At the discretion of the commanding officer, election candidates are permitted to visit Service Family Accommodation situated inside defence establishments, to canvass Service personnel and their families or to take electors to the polling stations. Canvassing in Single Living Accommodation (SLA) is not permitted. If a candidate requests permission to canvass Service personnel living inside a defence establishment, then, at the discretion of the Commanding Officer, a communal space within the establishment may be made available to allow Service personnel (particularly those living in SLA) who wish to hear the candidate to do so. Commanding Officers, taking operational and security considerations into account, are to ensure that no bias is shown for or against any political party that makes such a request.

If one party or candidate is granted a facility, then all other parties or candidates asking for the same would have to be granted the same facility. Where permission to visit a Service establishment is granted, it is to be made clear to the candidate that the visit may take place only on the condition that no members of the Armed Forces are to be used for political advantage; there will be no media involvement, nor should the visit be used to generate any publicity including use of private images and/or quotes on promotional material or websites. Service personnel whose duties do not preclude them from attending a meeting with a candidate should be allowed to do so. Uniform should not be worn unless otherwise unavoidable.

Any correspondence from candidates, constituency parties or other party bodies with requests to visit defence establishments other than Service Family Accommodation should be forwarded through the appropriate MOD Secretariat for a response. The originator should be informed that Ministerial approval is being sought. Cabinet Office provides guidance on elections, so please contact the Permanent Secretary’s office for any further guidance required.

Reservists

There will be parliamentarians who are also members of the Reserve forces. It is important that the roles in which parliamentarians are engaged as Service personnel are clear and that there is no blurring of the distinction between their parliamentary and Reserve responsibilities. Approval can be sought from Ministers by contacting the Ministers Private Office. It would be inappropriate for briefing provided to an individual as a member of the Reserve Forces to then be used for parliamentary or political purposes.

Reservists must not use information obtained through reserve service for parliamentary or political purposes. This includes:

information learned during reserve duties

contact details obtained through reserve service

relationships established through reserve service

decisions or public statements based on information obtained through reserve service, whether or not that information is explicitly referenced

If there is a potential conflict of interest, or if advice is needed, contact Parliamentary Branch and Ministers’ Private Office.
